metadata.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump mail ballot restrictions for now ahead of midterms

sources.news_title: The ruling keeps states using existing mail-ballot procedures while legal challenges continue, after judges said the Postal Service lacked authority and time was short.

Justices Reject Mail Ballot Changes
CNN 5 Things

Local experts weighed in on the court's decision.
CHICAGO (WLS) -- With the midterms just seven weeks away, the Supreme Court dealt a blow to President Trump, blocking attempts to limit mail-in voting.
"Elections will proceed as they always would have," ABC7 Legal Analyst Gil Soffer said.
The president's plan had required states to adopt a uniform envelope style and submit lists of eligible voters to a portal run by the Postal Service. Now, the new rules are frozen.
"The Supreme Court says we're not going to interfere; we're going to let the process proceed as it will without the new rules in effect," Soffer said.
It clears the way for states to send mail-in ballots ahead of the midterms.
"What we want is everybody that's eligible - Republican, Democrat, or Independent - to be able to go vote," Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker told Eyewitness News on Tuesday.
He vowed to continue pushing back against Trump.
SEE ALSO | Trump slams the Supreme Court for rejecting his push to restrict mail ballots
"Donald Trump wants to stand in the way of you exercising your right as a citizen in Illinois. We're trying to make it so that you can exercise that right," Pritzker said.
Trump blasted the high court's decision, saying it's a big loss for Republicans and criticizing the justices themselves.
"These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "They are merely a shell of their original selves."
With vote-by-mail ballots just days away from arriving in mailboxes, Tuesday marks National Voter Registration Day.
Cook County Clerk Monica Gordon appeared with rap artist Che "Rhymefest" Smith in a new video targeted toward young voters.
"I think this is an attempt to get the word out as early as possible to encourage younger people to vote," ABC7 Political Analyst Laura Washington said.
Washington said participation in midterm elections is historically low and usually brings out party loyalists.
"The casual voters often stay at home, so there are going to be a lot of attempts to get people energized beyond the usual suspects, and get them out to vote on both sides of the aisle," Washington said.
Washington also said the debate surrounding vote-by-mail ballots is not over and predicted it will pick up again for the presidential election.

RALEIGH, N.C. (WTVD) -- A U.S. Supreme Court ruling has cleared the way for absentee voting to continue without newly implemented rules for the upcoming midterm elections, rejecting an effort by the Trump administration to impose those restrictions on the mail-in ballot process.
"It just affirms what we've always known. The president trying to make rules at the last minute, on an emergency basis, was never going to fly, not even with this court," said Brooks Fuller, Director of Common Cause North Carolina.
In a 7-2 decision, the court found the government is "unlikely to succeed on the merits" of its challenge.
"The states have the right, according to the US Constitution, to run elections," said James Carter, President of the National Bar Association. "And by placing this artificial barrier, having the United States Postal Service verify names, etc., and put barcodes, etc., this is an unnecessary and unconstitutional barrier."
Absentee ballots have already been sent out in North Carolina, with some votes even being returned.
In a statement, a spokesperson for the North Carolina Board of Elections wrote:
"While the NCSBE has been monitoring any legal actions taken at the federal level, yesterday's ruling doesn't really affect our processes. Our counties continue to send, receive and process mail-in ballots through Election Day."
The Trump administration had sought to require states to provide voter lists, including names, addresses and barcodes, to the U.S. Postal Service. Under the proposal, the Postal Service would only deliver absentee ballots to voters appearing on those lists. Supporters argued the change would enhance election security, while critics contended it represented an unconstitutional federal intrusion into elections traditionally administered by states.
While it is not clear whether the Trump administration will ultimately seek to present oral arguments to the Supreme Court, Carter believes the ruling would be unchanged.
"In a live Supreme Court circumstance, you will have differing and more intimate ability to present arguments in ways that sometimes can't be communicated on paper. Live court proceedings allow one to read the room in certain ways, to see if a particular Justice is leaning a particular way, and maybe you adjust one's argument based upon that. I do believe though, the substance of the matter here is so great (and) I think the Supreme Court's guidance from the U.S. Constitution is so great here that I think it's going to leave very little room for whether or not there's different types of modalities that one can use from an eloquence perspective to change the ruling in this particular situation," said Carter.
Before the Supreme Court ruling, a federal judge had blocked the restrictions from moving forward.
In a statement, North Carolina Attorney General wrote:
"In a 7-2 vote, the Supreme Court just agreed with us that the Postal Service's last-minute changes to mail-in voting were a recipe for chaos. Ballots in North Carolina have already started going out and coming back. The election is underway. It would have been impossible for the Postal Service to implement a whole new system in time for the election - especially since the new system doesn't even exist yet. As Justice Kavanaugh put it, "state and local officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections." We appreciate the Court recognizing the practical reality of the situation. Voting has begun. You don't change the rules in the middle of the election."
President Trump criticized the Supreme Court, writing in part:
"Republicans just got another bad decision from the United States Supreme Court, one that the Court System took forever to give, and then blamed it, in part, on no time left to implement a solution."
Earlier this month, the North Carolina State Board of Elections enacted changes to how absentee ballots must be submitted.
In 2022, 187,746 North Carolinians voted absentee by mail. Voting rights advocates have expressed concern about how new policies could potentially confuse voters.
"I think that voting rights advocates all over the state are breathing a small sigh of relief," Fuller said. "It's good that these rules are not changing at the very last minute."

Supreme Court keeps USPS from carrying out mail-in voting changes in midterm elections
Postmaster General David Steiner previously told Government Executive that USPS would comply if the courts decided to block these changes.
The Supreme Court is keeping the Trump administration from imposing new rules for mail-in ballots in the lead-up to the midterm elections this November.
President Donald Trump signed an executive order in March imposing new rules on mail-in voting. The Postal Service released a final rule in August to implement the executive order.
The court’s tersely worded and unsigned order issued Monday evening states that the government “is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge” to a lower court's preliminary injunction that barred USPS from taking further steps to carry out its final rule.
The final rule would have required states planning to send mail-in or absentee ballots to provide USPS with a list of participating voters. The final rule also established new barcode and envelope-formatting requirements.
USPS previously provided nonbinding guidance to states on envelopes and barcodes in previous elections, but its final rule would have allowed the agency to reject ballots that didn’t meet its standards. USPS was also tasked under the executive order with launching a Federal Mail Ballot Portal for states to upload their voter lists.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in his concurring opinion that "there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service’s statutory authority," but that applying the final rule to this year’s elections would be “arbitrary and capricious” under the Administrative Procedures Act, “because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections.”
Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, in their dissent, wrote that the “Postal Service has broad authority to regulate the mail,” and that without a stay of the lower court’s ruling, the government “will suffer irreparable harm." The USPS final rule, they argued, would have increased the visibility of ballots in transit and would have helped “better detect election fraud.”
Postmaster General David Steiner told Government Executive in an exclusive interview last month that USPS “is not a political organization,” and would comply if the courts decided to permanently block the executive order's implementation.
“We deliver the mail. Someone else makes the rules. We deliver the mail, and so we deliver the mail under the rules that are put on us, and that's exactly what we'll do. People can fight over whether the rules are valid or not. Once that fight is finished, we'll do whatever the courts say we can do. That's not our decision,” Steiner said.
The American Postal Workers Union, which represents the frontline USPS employees most directly impacted by the final rule, warned that its employees hadn’t received training on changes outlined in the executive order or USPS final rule.
In an amicus curiae brief, the union warned that the final rule would “likely cause catastrophic wholesale non-delivery of mail to hundreds of thousands of voters,” because postal clerks “cannot realistically be trained" on these changes ahead of the November elections.
APWU represents the frontline Business Mail Entry Unit (BMEU) clerks who accept large batches of mail-in ballots to be delivered to voters. Under the final rule, postal clerks would have scanned a sample of each batch of ballots to confirm the voter information on individual ballots matches the information states submitted to the online portal.
A USPS whistleblower claimed that if clerks identified any errors in the sample, USPS would have refused to accept the entire batch - in many cases, tens of thousands of ballots - until election officials resolved the errors.
APWU also represents the IT workers tasked with creating that online portal. The USPS whistleblower also claimed that the agency has rushed to complete work on the portal, and hasn’t followed “standard principles of testing and debugging new software before launch.”

This story is adapted from the Slatest newsletter. You can sign up here to get it in your inbox every day.
On Monday, the Supreme Court blocked Donald Trump’s effort to throw mail balloting into chaos ahead of the November midterm elections. But that was just one prong of Trump’s attempts to tilt races toward Republicans. Today we’ll explain the others.
This Supreme Court ruling seems like a big deal. What exactly happened?
You aren’t wrong. As the legal expert Richard Hasen explains in Slate, Trump’s executive order would have created onerous new requirements for mail-in voting that risked disenfranchising millions of elderly, military, and other voters. Seven of nine justices apparently saw that potential catastrophe coming and rejected it, prompting a Tuesday-morning tantrum from the president. Trump has repeatedly tried to get the court to take his side on mail-in ballots, but this ruling looks like the end of the line—at least for this year’s elections.
OK, bullet dodged. But what else is Trump doing that we should worry about?
Trump’s order was backed by his unfounded claims that mail voting is fraudulent, part of his broader obsession with the false notion that Democrats are “cheating” to win elections. Trump has said he wants to “take over” elections, which are currently administered by state-level officials. That decentralized system is actually a bulwark against the kind of cheating Trump claims to care about—and against a sore-loser president trying to change election rules to protect his own interests. Still, Trump’s administration is trying to get states to hand over voter data and hunting through the rolls for alleged fraud.
What have they found?
It’s true that individuals have sometimes illegally cast ballots. But many of those cases have been accidents, like when a software error in New Jersey improperly registered noncitizens in 2023 and 2024, and widespread fraud is a myth. Per the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank that helped write Project 2025, there have been about 100 cases of noncitizen voting over the past 25 years.
Nevertheless, the administration has asked almost every state to turn over databases that include voters’ personal information. Most have resisted, sparking court battles that the administration has overwhelmingly lost. The Department of Homeland Security, meanwhile, has assigned hundreds of employees to parse public voting databases for noncitizens. Some have allegedly posed as voters, potentially violating state privacy laws. Yet Secretary Markwayne Mullin has publicly touted unverified numbers of alleged noncitizen voters and threatened election officials with prison time.
But surely those efforts can be contested in court?
Democrats and voting-rights groups have already sued over some of Trump’s moves (hence the case rejecting his mail ballot order). But some fear the administration is looking for ways to circumvent courts. Late last month, a whistleblower alleged that the U.S. Postal Service had continued to build an online portal that could’ve thrown out mail ballots en masse despite an order blocking work on it. (The Postal Service claims it hasn’t defied any court orders.)
What’s the bigger picture?
Courts can’t stop Trump from sowing doubt about the soundness of American elections. He has ordered investigations into debunked voting irregularities in states he lost in 2020 and continues to attack voting machines despite there being no evidence that they’ve ever changed election results. That could lay the groundwork to claim there was fraud if certain races don’t go Republicans’ way this fall. And even if judges toss those claims, they may still depress faith in the results. One recent survey found that less than half of Americans expect the midterms to be free and fair, with most Republicans doubting that mailed ballots are counted accurately and most Democrats fearful that Trump will deploy immigration agents to polling places. So, while the voting could ultimately go off without a hitch, the crisis of confidence continues.
The midterms are still several weeks away, so let’s turn to a more urgent question: How to enjoy the rest of your evening. My colleagues have some ideas that don’t require an appeal to the Supreme Court.

Reconsider your “smart” home: Cameras are becoming more and more common in home appliances, including in smart ovens, refrigerators, doorbells, and toothbrushes—even as people decry surveillance measures in public. What does this trend mean for our consumption? Steffi Cao has a prediction.
